title: -DIr: assumption and authority
intro: You have met `-DIr` twice: for how long something has lasted, *üç yıldır* ([A2 unit 9](gp-duration-dir)), and as the formal **is** of notices and definitions ([B2 unit 5](gp-dir-formal)). This unit adds its last two jobs. In conversation it turns a statement into a confident assumption: *Yorulmuşlardır* (They'll be tired by now). In writing it is the voice of authority, the encyclopedia's `-mIştIr`. The unit ends by lining up every way you know of saying how sure you are.

blocks.text: Said by a person about something they haven't checked, `-DIr` sounds like a confident assumption, close to English **will** or **must**: *Ali şimdi evdedir* (Ali will be at home by now), *Postacıdır* (That'll be the postman). It goes on a noun, an adjective or a place, or after a tense with its person ending.

**After `-mIş`** it is a guess about the past, much like `-mIş olmalı` ([unit 1](gp-mis-olmali)): *Toplantı bitmiştir* (The meeting will have ended by now), *Bu haberi duymuşsundur* (You'll have heard this news). The type I ending comes first, then `-DIr`, which follows harmony and turns d into t after a voiceless consonant.

blocks.title: *duymak*: I must have heard, you'll have heard…

rows.en: he, she or it will have heard
he, she or it probably hasn't heard
you probably haven't heard (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **Questions** with `-DIr` are uncommon. With *acaba* they voice a wondering, mostly in the third person, and the particle comes before `-DIr`: *Acaba duymuş mudur?* (I wonder if he's heard), *Acaba evde midir?* (Would she be at home, I wonder?).

head: Question
Meaning
rows: Would she be at home, I wonder?
Could they have forgotten us, I wonder?

blocks.text: **With `-(I)yor` and the future.** *Şu an uyuyordur* (He'll be asleep right now). After the future, `-DIr` adds confidence rather than doubt: *Merak etme, gelecektir* (Don't worry, he'll come).

items.tr: Saat on bir oldu; çocuklar uyumuştur.
items.seg: Saat on bir ol|du; çocuk|lar uyu|muş|tur.
items.en: It's eleven o'clock: the children will be asleep by now.
You'll have seen this film too.
Ayşe will be at the office at this time.
Could they have forgotten us, I wonder?

items.tr: Merak etme, yolu bulur; mutlaka bir haritası vardır.
items.seg: Merak et|me, yol|u bul|ur; mutlaka bir harita|s|ı var|dır.
items.en: Don't worry, he'll find the way: he's bound to have a map.

blocks.text: Context decides between the two `-DIr`s. On a notice, *Müze kapalıdır* states a fact: **the museum is closed**. Said by a friend outside the museum at nine at night, *Müze kapalıdır* is a guess: **the museum will be closed**.
*Yorulmuştur* (he'll be tired; in writing, he got tired) is not *yorulmuştu* (he had got tired, [B1 unit 1](gp-pluperfect)). One letter changes the meaning.
In the first person, `-mIşImdIr` often exaggerates or concedes: *Bunu sana yüz kere söylemişimdir* (I must have told you this a hundred times).

Encyclopedias, textbooks, museum labels and academic papers put `-DIr` on statements of fact. For the past they use `-mIştIr` where speech uses `-DI`: *Hitit Devleti'nin başkenti Hattuşa'dır* (The capital of the Hittite state is Hattusa); *Hititler Mezopotamya kökenli çivi yazısını kullanmışlardır* (The Hittites used cuneiform, a script that came from Mesopotamia). Here `-mIştIr` neither guesses nor passes on hearsay: it states, impersonally, what is established.

head: Speech
Writing
Meaning
rows: The two kings signed the treaty.
Hattusa was the capital for a long time.
Bu, bilinen en eski Hint-Avrupa dili.
Bu, bilinen en eski Hint-Avrupa dilidir.
This is the oldest known Indo-European language.
The city emptied little by little.

blocks.text: **Plural subjects.** For people, the plural ending comes before `-DIr`: *Hititler … kullanmışlardır*. Things usually keep the singular: *Tabletler 1906'da bulunmuştur*.

**Other tenses.** `-mAktAdIr` ([B2 unit 5](gp-makta)) for what is ongoing, `-(y)AcAktIr` for what will happen, and the aorist for laws of nature: *Su yüz derecede kaynar* (Water boils at a hundred degrees), against the definition *Suyun kaynama noktası yüz derecedir* (The boiling point of water is a hundred degrees).

**How firmly is it known?** Academic Turkish hangs a passive verb of knowing or thinking, in `-mAktAdIr`, on a noun clause ([B2 unit 4](gp-dik-clauses)). The verb tells the reader how firm the claim is.

head: Phrase
Meaning
Strength
rows: a claim the writer doesn't vouch for

items.tr: Hitit dili, bilinen en eski Hint-Avrupa dilidir.
items.seg: Hitit dil|i, bil|in|en en eski Hint-Avrupa dil|i|dir.
items.en: Hittite is the oldest known Indo-European language.

items.tr: Arşivde yaklaşık 25.000 tablet bulunduğu tahmin edilmektedir.
items.seg: Arşiv|de yaklaşık 25.000 tablet bul|un|duğ|u tahmin ed|il|mekte|dir.
items.en: The archive is estimated to hold about 25,000 tablets.
The city is believed to have been destroyed by a fire.
The Hittites used chariots with great skill.

blocks.text: The same form, two voices. In a textbook, *Hititler çivi yazısını kullanmışlardır* states a fact. From a colleague, *Ali çoktan gitmiştir* is an assumption: **Ali will have left long ago**. Who is speaking, and where, tells you which.

sections.title: Herhâlde, muhtemelen, mutlaka: how sure are you?

blocks.text: A sentence adverb sets the speaker's confidence. Most go at the start of the sentence or just before the verb, and they combine freely with `-DIr` and with the forms of [unit 1](gp-mis-olmali): *Mutlaka duymuşsundur* (You must surely have heard), *Büyük ihtimalle gitmiştir* (She has most likely left).

head: Adverb
Meaning
Strength
Register
rows: everywhere; olasılık is a little more formal

blocks.text: **Herhâlde** is a supposition: *Herhâlde trafiğe takıldı* (I suppose she got stuck in traffic). **Galiba** often rests on something you've noticed: *Galiba yağmur yağacak* (Looks like it's going to rain). **Sanırım** gives your opinion; it comes from *sanmak* ([A2 unit 4](gp-aorist-irregulars)), and its negative *Sanmıyorum* is **I don't think so**.

**Belki de** brings in a new possibility, often after others: *Belki de haklısın* (Maybe you're right after all). **Mutlaka** with a guess means **surely**; with an imperative or a plan it means **without fail**: *Mutlaka gel* (Be sure to come).

**Written synonyms.** Careful and academic Turkish often prefers *olası* (possible, likely) and *olasılık* (probability) to everyday *mümkün* and *ihtimal*: *olası bir sonuç* (a possible outcome), *büyük olasılıkla* (most likely). *Tahminen* is **at a guess, roughly**, usually before a number: *tahminen üç bin kişi* (roughly three thousand people).

items.en: You must surely have heard: everyone's talking about it.
I suppose she missed the bus.
The meeting will most likely be postponed.

blocks.text: Don't mix strengths that pull apart: *Kesinlikle gelmiş olabilir* is self-contradictory. Say *Kesinlikle gelmiştir* if you're sure, *Belki de gelmiştir* if you're not.
On its own, with an ironic tone, *Herhâlde!* means **Obviously!**: — *Geliyor musun?* — *Herhâlde!* (Are you coming? Of course I am!).

sections.title: Geldi, gelmiş, gelmiştir: from certain to guessed

blocks.text: Turkish marks in the verb how you know what you say. Here are the forms you've met, from what you saw to what you merely suppose.

head: Form
Example
What the speaker claims
rows: I know it: I saw it, or it's common knowledge.
I heard it, or I see the result: his coat is here.
I'm confident: he always comes at eight.
I think so, but I'm not sure.

blocks.text: `-mIştIr` and `-mIş olmalı` are close, and many speakers use them interchangeably. Roughly, `-DIr` leans on what you know of the world or the person (*Her sabah sekizde gelir; şimdiye gelmiştir*), and `-mIş olmalı` on clues in front of you (*Ceketi burada; gelmiş olmalı*).
**In writing**, the same scale appears in fuller forms, and a historian gives each claim the weight it deserves.

head: Claim
Weight
rows: Kentin bir saldırıyla yıkıldığı da iddia edilmektedir.
a claim the writer doesn't endorse

items.tr: Kapı açık; biri içeri girmiş olmalı.
items.seg: Kapı açık; biri içeri gir|miş ol|malı.
items.en: The door is open: someone must have gone in.

items.tr: Ayşe her zaman erken gelir; şimdiye gelmiştir.
items.seg: Ayşe her zaman erken gel|ir; şimdiye gel|miş|tir.
items.en: Ayşe always comes early: she'll be here by now.
The neighbours told me: Ali has moved, apparently.
The queen may have written the letter herself.

blocks.text: Translating into English, let the Turkish form choose the English one: *geldi* **he came**, *gelmiş* **apparently he came**, *gelmiştir* **he'll have come** (in a textbook simply **he came**), *gelmiş olmalı* **he must have come**, *gelmiş olabilir* **he may have come**. [C1 unit 7](gp-meger) adds *meğer*, for finding out what was true all along.

summary: In conversation, `-DIr` after a noun, a place or a tense is a confident assumption: *Evdedir*, *Uyuyordur*, *Duymuşsundur*.
The type I ending comes before `-DIr`: *duymuşsundur*, *yorulmuşlardır*; with *acaba*, *mI* comes before it: *duymuş mudur?*
In encyclopedias and academic writing, `-DIr` states facts and `-mIştIr` is the neutral past: *Hattuşa'dır*, *kullanmışlardır*.
*Bilinmektedir*, *kabul edilmektedir*, *tahmin edilmektedir*, *düşünülmektedir*, *sanılmaktadır* and *iddia edilmektedir* tell how firmly a claim is held.
*Kesinlikle* and *mutlaka* are near certain, *muhtemelen* and *büyük ihtimalle* probable, *herhâlde*, *sanırım* and *galiba* softer, *belki de* weakest.
From certain to guessed: *geldi*, *gelmiş*, *gelmiştir*, *gelmiş olmalı*, *galiba geldi*, *gelmiş olabilir*.
